items.abstract_or_text: Complex systems exhibit organization not only through their components but also via their interdependencies. Local nucleotide dependencies underpin regulatory motifs and RNA structures, yet principles governing a higher-order organization across the human genome remain unknown. Here we systematically perturbed every position of the com- plete telomere-to-telomere human genome using Nucleotide Transformer v3 with an ex- ascale compute cluster, generating nucleotide-resolution dependency maps that reveal a directed, weighted network of position-to-position genomic relationships. This network recapitulates known biological features and uncovers recurrent, directional architec- tures termed 'relons', spanning coding, non-coding, and unannotated regions. These re- lational modules reflect evolutionary and functional constraints and associate with hu- man genetic variation and pathogenic variants. Our findings suggest a higher-order rela- tional layer of genome organization, providing a framework to interpret DNA as a complex system of dependencies beyond linear and 3D structure, with implications for under- standing genetic variation and disease.

items.title: Lipid nanoparticle-mediated RNAi targeting of KRAS mutants sensitises colorectal cancer cells to chemotherapy
items.abstract_or_text: KRAS mutations, including G12D, G12V and G13D, are major oncogenic drivers in colorectal cancer (CRC) and are associated with therapeutic resistance. However, approved KRAS inhibitors remain focused on G12C subtype, leaving these prevalent variants without approved targeted therapies. Here, we developed a lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based RNA interference (RNAi) strategy to target these three KRAS variants using a single small interfering RNA (siRNA) sequence. The developed siRNA-LNPs reduced KRAS mRNA and protein expression in HCT116 (G13D), SW620 (G12V) and LS180 (G12D) cells, but not in KRAS wild-type HT29 cells, suppressing the cellular proliferation, clonogenic survival and migration. Transcriptomic profiling revealed changes in KRAS associated signalling, including suppression of cell-cycle and DNA repair programmes, providing a rationale for combining siRNA silencing with the fluoropyrimidine chemotherapeutic agent 5-fluorouracil (5-FU). The combination produced synergistic effects across all three KRAS-mutant CRC cell models and enhanced the apoptosis in both monolayer cultures and 3D spheroids. Collectively, these findings provide proof of concept for this combination strategy and support its further investigation as a potential therapeutic approach for KRAS-mutant CRC.

items.title: Selective vulnerability: validation of atypical neurodegenerative disease variants in histopathological reference cohorts
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Objective: Standard guidelines for neurodegenerative diseases rely on cohort-level criteria, frequently misclassifying isolated atypical phenotypes. This study tests whether atypical variants mirror topographically determined systemic central nervous system (CNS) conditions rooted in pre-existing vulnerability. Methods: Using "reverse-matching", phenotypes from six atypical cases—representing motor neuron disease/frontotemporal dementia ( N = 3) and multiple system atrophy, parkinsonian type ( N = 3)—were mapped onto a protein-agnostic network matrix (onto-phylogenetic coordinate system, OPC; Geser 2026). Spatial network recruitment was quantified using Jaccard coefficients ( J ). Spearman rank correlations ( ρ ) evaluated systemic hierarchies against conventional reference matrices (Geser 2008 cohort, TDP-43, N = 31; Jellinger 2005 cohort, α-synuclein, N = 42). Model comparison was performed using Steiger’s Z -test. Results: Conventional, cohort-based staging exhibited profound topographical inversion, yielding negative correlations for TDP-43 ( ρ = -0.9113, p ρ = -0.8660, p = 0.003) sub-cohorts. Conversely, the novel OPC system resolved this mismatch, reversing the correlation into a highly precise positive range (TDP-43: ρ = 0.9113, p R 2 = 0.83; α-synuclein: ρ = 0.8660, p = 0.003, R 2 = 0.75). In the combined pool ( N = 18 data pairs), the OPC model achieved strong global validation ( ρ = 0.8825, p R 2 = 0.78; Steiger Z = -6.497, p J = 1.00). Interpretation: Atypical variants are not statistical outliers but topographically determined systemic states reflecting inherent CNS vulnerability. Clinical anomalies serve as highly sensitive, topographically anchored early indicators ("red flags") of underlying proteinopathies.

items.title: International Multi-Centre Validation of Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Precise Discrimination between Normal and Abnormal Retinal Development
items.abstract_or_text: Arrested retinal development can cause childhood visual impairment, but grading optical coherence tomography scans is difficult to standardise across devices and centres. We developed and evaluated an unsupervised domain adaptation model to classify normal and abnormal retinal development across different OCT systems. This retrospective multicentre study used OCT scans from five centres in four countries and the UK Biobank. Data covered four OCT devices, including table mounted and handheld systems. A ResNet50 based Domain Adversarial Neural Network was trained using labelled images from a source device and unlabelled images from a target device. We evaluated six source to target pairings and compared model performance with seven clinician graders. A separate Heidelberg Spectralis dataset was reserved for external evaluation. Across validation sets, accuracy ranged from 87.75% to 96.06%, sensitivity from 88.68% to 98.38%, and specificity from 78.00% to 98.02%. The best performing model, adapted from TM OCT1 to HH OCT1, achieved 96.06% accuracy and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.994, with a 95% confidence interval from 0.981 to 0.999. Several models also maintained discrimination on the unseen Heidelberg device. Unsupervised domain adaptation enabled OCT classification across devices without labelled target device data. The approach may support more consistent assessment of retinal development and large scale analysis of existing imaging datasets.

items.title: SciΠvot: Benchmarking Principal-Investigator Judgment at Pivotal Moments of Scientific AutoResearch Agents
items.abstract_or_text: Large language model (LLM) agents can keep scientific experiments running for months with little human supervision, but reliable autonomous research also requires scientific judgment. Evaluating scientific judgment is difficult because research decisions are open-ended and depend on project context. We construct SciΠvot, a 248-case benchmark of scientific judgment based on human corrections. The benchmark draws on records from six months of research in which senior researchers ran LLM agents on 26 projects across six scientific fields and repeatedly intervened to correct the agents' research judgments. In each case, an agent chooses between the original LLM plan and the human-corrected alternative, using only the project record available before the correction as context. We compare LLM and human performance and examine the effects of reasoning effort, access to the project record, and reconsideration. At medium reasoning effort with the project record, models systematically prefer the original LLM plan over the human-corrected alternative. Four of five frontier models perform below chance on the selected cases. The highest accuracy in the project condition across the tested models and reasoning effort settings is 63.5%, compared with 73.4% for fresh researchers. At medium effort, every model achieves lower accuracy with the project record than without it, and reconsideration does not consistently improve overall accuracy. Even with a human-corrected alternative available, frontier models struggle with the selected research decisions, while SciΠvot supports systematic evaluation of scientific judgment for LLM agents.

items.title: Synthetic Aperture Radar, Multi-Source Data Fusion, and Machine Learning for Aboveground Biomass and Carbon Stock Estimation: A Systematic Review and Bibliometric Analysis
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Accurate estimation of aboveground biomass (AGB) and carbon stocks is fundamental for sustainable forest management, climate change mitigation, and ecosystem monitoring. Advances in synthetic aperture radar (SAR), multi-source remote sensing, and artificial intelligence have substantially improved biomass estimation; however, existing research remains methodologically fragmented, with limited synthesis of sensor fusion strategies, machine learning, and deep learning approaches, and their applicability to urban tree carbon estimation. This study presents a systematic review and bibliometric analysis of peer-reviewed literature published between 2004 and 2026 following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) guidelines. Literature was retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, screened using Rayyan, and 68 eligible studies were identified for qualitative synthesis. The review examined publication trends, geographical distribution, remote sensing platforms, data fusion strategies, machine learning and deep learning algorithms, validation approaches, and emerging research gaps. The findings reveal a substantial increase in publications after 2018, driven by the widespread availability of Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, LiDAR, cloud-based geospatial platforms, and advances in artificial intelligence. The reviewed literature demonstrates a clear transition from single-sensor approaches towards feature-level fusion of SAR, optical, and LiDAR data, which consistently improved biomass and carbon estimation compared with individual sensors. Among predictive models, ensemble learning algorithms, particularly Random Forest and Extreme Gradient Boosting, remained the most robust and widely adopted, while deep learning approaches showed increasing potential for high-resolution applications where sufficient training data were available. Despite these advances, research focusing specifically on urban tree biomass and carbon estimation remains limited, highlighting challenges related to heterogeneous urban environments, limited reference datasets, SAR integration, and model transferability. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of current methodological developments, identifies critical knowledge gaps, and proposes future research directions to develop robust, scalable, interpretable, and transferable frameworks for biomass and carbon estimation across natural and urban ecosystems.

items.title: BanglaDiaHallu: Hallucinations of large language models and the effect of guideline-grounded retrieval-augmented generation in Bangla diabetes question answering
items.abstract_or_text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted for health advice, but they can produce fluent statements that are false or unsupported, known as hallucinations, and this risk is poorly characterised in low-resource languages such as Bangla. We measured hallucinations of locally deployable open-weight LLMs in Bangla diabetes question answering and tested whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounded in Bangladesh’s National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus reduces them. Forty patient questions spanning six clinical sub-domains were each answered twice, under zero-shot prompting, by Qwen3.5-9B, TigerLLM-9B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B, and by BanglaDiaRAG, which adds hybrid dense (BGE-M3) and sparse (BM25) retrieval from a physician-reviewed Bangla guideline knowledge base to Qwen3.5-9B. Two physicians rated the 400 de-identified responses by consensus for medical accuracy, completeness, safety, readability and reliability on a 0–1 scale, and responses with accuracy below 0.70 were classified as hallucinated. Hallucination rates were 2.5% for Gemma-4-26B-A4B, 3.8% for TigerLLM-9B, 22.5% for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and 77.5% for Qwen3.5-9B. Guideline grounding lowered the rate of Qwen3.5-9B to 11.3% (difference −66.3 percentage points; 95% CI −76.3 to −55.0) and raised every criterion by 0.24 to 0.38 points (Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). BanglaDiaRAG outscored Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on all five criteria and matched or exceeded TigerLLM-9B, but it remained below Gemma-4-26B-A4B in safety, readability and reliability, and its residual errors were specific, confident and potentially harmful. Guideline grounding can turn a weak general-purpose model into a much safer Bangla diabetes assistant, but the choice of base model mattered as much as retrieval and no configuration was free of hallucination, so clinical oversight remains essential before patient-facing use.

items.title: C-MOP: A Narrative Review and Clinical Framework for Adjunctive Repurposed-Drug Therapy in Active Cancer
items.abstract_or_text: Cancer metabolic adaptability and treatment resistance provide a rationale for evaluating coordinated interventions across complementary tumor and host processes. This narrative review examines five medications used within the Cancer Metabolic Optimization Protocol (C-MOP) - metformin, atorvastatin, doxycycline, mebendazole, and ivermectin - and describes a physician-directed framework for adjunctive use in adults with active cancer. The central hypothesis is that complementary effects on energy regulation, mevalonate signaling, mitochondrial function, microtubule dynamics, and adaptive stress responses may constrain compensatory pathways and enhance sensitivity to conventional treatment. Selected experimental combinations and early clinical experience with other multi-agent repurposing regimens support investigation of this strategy. Evidence for the individual agents is heterogeneous: metformin and statins have the largest human evidence base, with mixed or negative randomized findings in several settings; doxycycline and mebendazole have predominantly preclinical, translational, and early-phase support. Ivermectin remains the most experimental component, with predominantly preclinical evidence and evolving dosing and long-term safety questions in oncology. The framework links agent selection to patient-specific goals, conventional oncology treatment, organ function, interactions, sequential initiation, monitoring, and reassessment of treatment burden. The clinical benefit of the complete five-agent regimen remains to be established. By defining the combination rationale, patient selection, individualized implementation, and safety procedures, C-MOP provides a foundation for consistent clinical reporting and prospective evaluation.

items.title: Documenting Trofinetide Treatment Phenotypes in Rett Syndrome with a Dual-LLM Consensus Pipeline
items.abstract_or_text: Objective: Trofinetide, approved in 2023 as the first Rett syndrome treatment, lacks scalable real-world monitoring because chart review is labor-intensive. We developed a dual large language model (LLM) consensus pipeline to extract 18 treatment-response phenotypes, comprising 4 adverse effects, 13 Rett clinical features, and medication refusal, from clinical notes. Materials and Methods: We analyzed 26,763 notes from 108 patients with confirmed sustained trofinetide exposure at Texas Children's Hospital. The pipeline filters notes by keyword, classifies each through two LLMs requiring consensus, and aggregates a patient-by-timepoint matrix. Architecture and prompt were selected on a diarrhea development set, then frozen and applied to the other 17 phenotypes with the phenotype definition substituted, as an out-of-sample test. The reported prompt comparison scores 183 expert-labeled cells. Results: A prompt requiring diarrhea to be active and severe performed best (84.2 \pm 0.0% accuracy; F1 = 0.674), 47 percentage points above regular-expression matching (p < 0.0001). Expert reviewers judged six of the pipeline's calls per phenotype, three positive and three negative, and agreed with 90.2% (92/102). The 13 Rett clinical features are manifestations of the disorder itself rather than adverse effects of trofinetide. Gross and fine motor impairment, language/communication, and stereotypy were documented present in 92-100% of patients at every visit. Discussion: In-context LLM extraction captured multi-domain treatment responses. The outcome is documented presence at each visit, not a direction-of-change judgment. Conclusion: Coupling in-context LLM reasoning with a consensus architecture offers a scalable alternative to keyword and regular-expression extraction for real-world evidence, adapting to new phenotypes and medications through configuration alone.

items.title: Predicting Live Birth After Fresh Embryo Transfer in IVF/ICSI: Differential ICM/Trophectoderm Morphology Encoding and a Hybrid Attention--Logistic Regression Ensemble
items.abstract_or_text: Predicting live birth before fresh embryo transfer could support shared decision-making in IVF/ICSI, but routine clinical data are small, heterogeneous, and contain pathway-dependent variables prone to outcome leakage. We aimed to construct a curated single-centre IVF/ICSI dataset and develop a prediction model suited to small tabular clinical data. Materials and Methods: We assembled 616 fresh embryo-transfer cycles (251 live birth, 365 non-live birth) with clinical, laboratory, and embryological predictors, and embryo morphology encoded with a novel differential weighting of the inner cell mass and trophectoderm. After KNN imputation, robust scaling, and selection of 50 features, we developed a Hybrid Attention Network (HAN), a learnable feature-attention gate followed by a compact multilayer perceptron, and a HAN + logistic-regression (LR) ensemble with a validation-tuned weight. Models were benchmarked against classical machine learning, TabPFN, and text-serialized language models on a held-out test set; AUC-ROC was the primary metric. Results: The HAN + LR ensemble achieved the highest test AUC-ROC (0.710; accuracy 0.710, F1 0.630), ahead of the HAN backbone alone (0.700), logistic regression (0.667), the TabPFN + LR hybrid (0.666), and TabPFN (0.650). Text-serialized language models performed near chance (AUC \le 0.61). The differentially weighted trophectoderm feature ranked highest by consensus importance across models. Discussion: A compact attention network combined with a linear model outperformed both components and strong foundation-model baselines on a small clinical cohort. Conclusion: The curated dataset and HAN + LR ensemble offer a transparent, reproducible basis for IVF/ICSI live-birth prediction; external validation is the next step.

items.title: OmicsBench: a long-horizon multi-turn benchmark of AI agents on research-study-scale bioinformatics
items.abstract_or_text: Computational biologists increasingly delegate substantial analyses to AI agents in long-horizon, multi-turn sessions, yet most benchmarks of agents' bioinformatics capabilities pose a single short task with a single-shot prompt. We present OmicsBench, a long-horizon, multi-turn bioinformatics benchmark for AI agents. Each of its 97 tasks links dependent subtasks into a directed acyclic graph, for 662 underlying subtasks in all. Each subtask is posed as one user turn and graded deterministically against an answer key, with optional in-context feedback on incorrect answers. Across 12 models on three harnesses, the slowest agent averages 3.6 hours per task, and no combination comes near saturating the benchmark, with mean scores of 0.43 to 0.57 out of a possible 1 without in-context feedback and 0.54 to 0.67 with it. Multi-turn evaluation also uncovers behavior that single-shot prompts cannot, as agents score lower on subtasks that depend on earlier subtasks, and in-context feedback helps agents recover some of that loss. Because deterministic scoring gives no qualitative account of how an agent failed, we also introduce an unsupervised failure mode discovery pipeline that describes, embeds, and clusters agents' failed attempts to surface emergent failure modes. Applied to OmicsBench, this pipeline exposes qualitative shortcomings in how agents carry out bioinformatics analyses, ranging from agents applying their own statistical filters in place of the specified ones to agents writing whole answers from memory.

items.title: Diagnostic accuracy of deep learning for microsatellite instability prediction in gastric cancer: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract_or_text: Deep learning (DL) applied to haematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained pathology images can predict microsatellite instability (MSI) in gastric cancer (GC). We evaluated its diagnostic accuracy and discriminative performance. PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library and Web of Science were searched for studies applying DL to H&E images for MSI prediction in GC. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261503140). Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were estimated with a bivariate random-effects model, with subgroup analyses by validation strategy and data source; slide-level areas under the curve (AUCs) were pooled after logit transformation. Prespecified scenario analyses assessed robustness. Ten studies were included; seven independent datasets from six studies entered the primary synthesis. Pooled sensitivity, specificity and summary receiver operating characteristic AUC were 0.78 (95% CI 0.63-0.88), 0.85 (95% CI 0.77-0.90) and 0.89 (95% CI 0.86-0.91); nine studies contributed to the secondary AUC synthesis (pooled AUC 0.85, 95% CI 0.80-0.89). Hospital-derived cohorts showed numerically higher sensitivity (0.86) and diagnostic odds ratio (39.8) than TCGA-derived cohorts (0.71 and 11.5), but subgroup differences were limited by the small number of studies and substantial heterogeneity. DL models show good diagnostic accuracy for MSI prediction in GC, but clinical utility still requires confirmation in standardised multicentre, independent external and prospective studies.

items.title: CAPO: Compute-Aware Automated Protein-Model Optimization
items.abstract_or_text: Protein models such as Evolutionary Scale Modeling (ESM), AlphaFold and Boltz have transformed computational protein science, yet a pretrained model rarely transfers to a particular laboratory's assay without adaptation to its data and experimental setting, and that adaptation is technically demanding and spends real compute budget. Existing agentic systems can automate model training, yet typically treat fine-tuning as a reliable tool call: feasibility and cost are estimated rather than measured, and infeasibility is discovered only after compute has been spent. We formulate protein-model adaptation as a gated decision problem: given a task, raw data and a compute budget c_max, a system should decide whether and how to adapt a model before committing expensive computation. We introduce CAPO (Compute-Aware Automated Protein-Model Optimization), a multi-agent system built around one rule: gate before you train. CAPO measures feasibility on the target accelerator, projects cost against the available budget, runs a canary inside the actual training loop and maintains an auditable artifact trail; critically, it can decline an unaffordable adaptation and select a cheaper alternative. We evaluate CAPO, without system changes, on three protein-modeling tasks: (i) SARS-CoV-2 host-range prediction, (ii) hit-to-lead affinity ranking and (iii) temporal variant-effect reclassification. On host range, CAPO partially fine-tuned an 8-million-parameter ESM-2 model to a species-averaged MCC of 0.826, compared with 0.743 for a hand-designed expert transformer; it matched a general coding agent while using 57.4% less GPU time and reduced failed training trials from four to zero. For hit-to-lead affinity ranking, CAPO rejected Boltz-2 fine-tuning and instead trained an assay-calibrated lightweight head over frozen representations, improving ranking on 11 of 15 held-out targets in 1.68 GPU-hours. On temporally held-out ClinVar variants, rank-4 low-rank adaptation of ESM-2 reached an MCC of 0.478, compared with 0.252 for a one-hot baseline and 0.000 for the frozen zero-shot score. These results come from single runs, without a gate ablation and with one generalist-agent comparison. Within those limits, they show that measured admission control can make protein-model adaptation not only automated but selective: deciding what to compute, what not to compute and why.

items.title: Network-enabled drug repurposing identifies lithium to promote cardiomyocyte proliferation
items.abstract_or_text: The adult mammalian heart has minimal regenerative capacity, limited in part by endogenous cardiomyocyte (CM) renewal. Although CM proliferation is a promising target in both congenital and adult heart disease, no current therapies specifically target this process. Progress has been hindered by the complexity of CM proliferation signaling networks, which may require systems-level approaches. The overall goal of this study was to leverage systems modeling to identify FDA approved drugs that have the potential to be repurposed towards CM proliferation. To achieve this goal, we developed a computational drug repurposing framework that integrates drug-target interaction data with a previously developed logic-based network model of CM proliferation signaling. Using this framework, we identified 81 drugs that directly target nodes within the CM proliferation network, corresponding to 32 unique drug-target interactions. Virtual screening predicted 5 unique drug-target interactions that increase CM proliferation and 14 that decrease CM proliferation outputs. Lithium, a GSK3{beta} inhibitor widely prescribed for bipolar disorder, was predicted and experimentally validated to promote CM proliferation through a Cyclin D/CDK4 pathway. In vivo, treatment of pregnant mice with lithium increased DNA synthesis in the CMs of their embryos. A retrospective analysis of the FDA Adverse Events Reporting System confirmed that relative to other mood stabilizers, in utero exposure to lithium was associated with an increased incidence of congenital heart defects, in males but not females. Together, this work provides a computational-experimental framework for repurposing FDA-approved drugs to modulate CM proliferation, which highlights therapeutic potential of lithium for adult CM regeneration but congenital risks to developing embryos.

items.title: EEG Pathology Detection via Clinical Concept Bottleneck Models
items.abstract_or_text: Deep learning models for electroencephalography (EEG) pathology detection achieve competitive accuracy but offer limited interpretability. In this paper, we introduce concept bottleneck models (CBMs) for EEG pathology detection which use clinical EEG biomarkers computed analytically from the signal as a bottleneck to be used for prediction. Those concepts include band power, spectral ratios, alpha peak frequency and amplitude, hemispheric asymmetry and phase locking values. With the backbone based on shallow convolutional neural network (CNN), we compare a black box baseline with two variants of CBMs. The hybrid variant is a classifier receives a residual projection of the backbone features. The pure variant is a CBM where the classifier receives only the predicted concepts. Models are evaluated on abnormality detection and dementia classification followed by concept prediction quality and leakage analysis. Both CBMs approach the baseline on TUAB (82.7-82.9% vs 83.6%) and are 2-5 percentage points lower on CAUEEG (57.9-60.5% vs 62.7%). The pure CBM exhibits concept fidelity concern where the predicted concepts deviate from their ground truth values. Replacing them with their true values causes severe cost on accuracy by 26 and 22 points on TUAB and CAUEEG. The concept fidelity concern is mitigated by increasing the weight of the concept loss to match the ground truth concepts. the mitigation comes with small accuracy cost on TUAB but a relatively larger cost on CAUEEG. The code of the experiments and full logs are available at https://www.github.com/mhmdrdwn/cbm.

items.title: Automated Dental Calculus Mapping and Burden Estimation Using Deep Learning
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Dental calculus is a primary etiological factor in periodontal disease, disproportionately affecting underserved populations with limited access to professional dental care. Automated photographic oral disease screening tools may help bridge this access gap by enabling early identification of calculus burden in community, school-based, and remote settings. Methods A ResNet-50 encoder integrated within a U-Net segmentation architecture was trained on intraoral photographic images sourced from a public dataset. The dataset was partitioned into training (1,361 images; 66.5%), validation (584 images; 28.5%), and an independent held-out test set (103 images; 5.0%), with the test set withheld from all model development decisions. Manual polygon segmentation masks were created using CVAT. A pixel-area calculation technique was developed to estimate the percentage of tooth surface covered by calculus. Architecture comparisons were conducted against a standard U-Net (no pretraining), VGG16/U-Net, and EfficientNet-B4/U-Net under identical training conditions. Results On the held-out test set, the model achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.731 (95% CI: 0.706–0.756), IoU of 0.698 (95% CI: 0.671–0.724), recall of 0.714, and specificity of 0.971. The pixel-level ROC-AUC was 0.931 (95% CI: 0.918–0.944) however, this value is inflated by background pixel dominance and should be interpreted alongside Dice and IoU as primary segmentation metrics. The proposed architecture outperformed all three comparators. Validation-set metrics (Dice 0.743, IoU 0.712) were modestly higher than test-set values, as expected given reduced optimization bias on unseen data. Conclusions This proof-of-concept study demonstrates that deep learning can support automated dental calculus screening from photographic images. Findings are preliminary and subject to important limitations including non-clinician annotation and a single public dataset source. With further clinical validation, such tools may contribute to scalable oral health monitoring in tele-dentistry workflows, school dental programs, and community health initiatives.

items.title: The Optimal Biological Therapy for Conversion in Patients with RAS Wild Type Colorectal Cancer and Unresectable Liver Metastases
items.abstract_or_text: Background: /Objectives: The treatment goal for patients with unresectable liver-limited metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) is resection. Biological agents directed to vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) and epidermal growth factor receptor (anti-EGFR) are effective in RAS wild type mCRC. We aimed to investigate which type of biological therapy is more efficient and tolerable in the first line treatment of patients with RAS wild type mCRC and unresectable liver metastases. Methods: This was a prospective, single-centre cohort analysis that included patients with mCRC and unresectable liver metastases, without mutations in the KRAS and NRAS genes (exons 2, 3 and 4), treated at the University Clinical Centre of Nis, Serbia. The overall response rate (ORR), depth of response (DoR), resection rate (RR), progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were compared between patients treated with the anti-EGFR antibody cetuximab/panitumumab and those treated with the anti-VEGF antibody bevacizumab, each in combination with the chemotherapy doublet FOLFOX/FOLFIRI. Results: Fifty-one patients were treated with anti-EGFR antibodies and 50 patients received bevacizumab. Anti-EGFR treatment provided better ORR (70.6% vs. 50%; p = 0.034), deeper response (47.2% vs. 33.67%; p = 0.004) and higher RR (66.7% vs. 46%; p=0.036). Median PFS was significantly better in the anti-EGFR treated group (12.1 vs. 8.5 months; p=0.016). Median OS tended to be better in anti-EGFR-treated patients, but the difference was not significant (30.4 vs. 25.5 months; p=0.221). Both treatments had comparable rates of grade 3/4 toxicity (37.2% vs. 28%; p=0.32). Conclusion: Patients with RAS wild-type, unresectable mCRC should be treated with anti-EGFR therapy when aiming for conversion.

items.title: Robust Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Treatment Regimes under Model and Measurement Uncertainty
items.abstract_or_text: We develop a robust reinforcement learning (RL) framework for learning adaptive treatment policies that generalize across patients and remain reliable under errors in the measured biomarker and shifts in the disease dynamics. By modeling the patient as a hidden context, we address generalization and robustness in a unified manner through robust contextual Markov decision processes. Applying our framework to adaptive therapy for metastatic prostate cancer in a simulator calibrated to clinical data, we obtain generalizable and robust policies that substantially outperform the existing adaptive therapy method. In particular, we attain robustness with almost no loss of performance when the biomarker is accurate and the disease evolves as anticipated, and find that the resulting policy Pareto-dominates the existing method across a diverse array of scenarios. Our findings suggest that robust RL holds great promise as a principled methodology for learning reliable adaptive treatment policies.

items.title: CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests
items.abstract_or_text: Context: Organizations increasingly delegate code review to multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipelines billed per token. Low code quality raises human maintenance effort, but its effect on agent review cost has not been measured. Objective: We test whether baseline CodeHealth predicts the token cost of agentic review and fix beyond pull request (PR) footprint. Method: In a pre-registered observational study, we sampled 465 agent-authored PRs from 246 repositories in AIDev, jointly stratified by CodeHealth and footprint under repository caps. A frozen five-agent review-and-fix pipeline processed every PR with three different LLMs. Per LLM, we fitted a mixed model of log tokens on CodeHealth and log PR footprint, with a repository random intercept. Results: For all three LLMs the CodeHealth coefficient was negative, with 95% CI excluding zero; each CodeHealth point was associated with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost. CodeHealth was unrelated to PR footprint, so PR size does not explain the association. Two of three registered smells predicted fix cost; batch fixing left median CodeHealth unchanged. Exploratory analyses located the association in the review stage, where agents iterated more on unhealthy code without writing more comments. Adjusting for the size of the scored files absorbed the association, which we interpret as mediation by file size. Conclusions: A quality metric calibrated against human maintainability also predicts the inference cost of multi-agent review and fix. The effect is modest per point and not carried by PR size, so the refactoring case extends to agent-reviewed code when it changes structure and file size, not only the score. items.title: ISW-Agent: Integrating LLM-Driven Dialogue with n8n Workflow for Internal Solitary Wave Remote Sensing Image Processing
items.abstract_or_text: Internal solitary wave (ISW) remote sensing requires task parameters and spatial information to be transferred across image acquisition, detection, stripe extraction, and propagation prediction. Here, we present ISW-Agent, which integrates large language model (LLM) interpretation with n8n workflows and independent scientific models through structured task constraints, geospatial transformations, and stage-specific output validation. In tests of 120 Chinese instructions per backend, GPT-5.6 Sol and DeepSeek both achieved a strict task-match rate of 94.2%, with all intents and execution decisions matching the reference. Sentinel-1 cases demonstrated continuous processing from dialogue requests to wavefront prediction for the specified scene. Of 50 timed scenes, 39 completed detection, extraction, and prediction with a median turnaround time of 48.04 s; 11 stopped after empty extraction. Across 3,408 controlled fault-injection runs, retries recovered 234 transient-failure conditions and output validation rejected 234 structural defects, while 61 provenance or completeness errors indicated the need for content-consistency checks. Overall, ISW-Agent thus connects natural-language requests to traceable spatial processing chains for multimodel ISW analysis.
